subjective.question: Define “virus” — what is meant by the word virus?
subjective.answer: Virus is a Latin word which means poison or venom. Viruses are noncellular particles made up of genetic material and proteins that can invade living cells.

subjective.question: What are viruses?
subjective.answer: Viruses are complicated assemblies of molecules, including proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates. Viruses can only replicate themselves by infecting a host cell and therefore cannot reproduce on their own.

subjective.question: Write down the general characteristics / properties of viruses. (3–5 marks)
subjective.answer: - A virus is a microscopic infectious agent that can only replicate inside the living cells of a host organism. - Viruses have a simple structure, consisting of genetic material (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid. Some viruses also have an outer envelope made up of lipids. - Viruses are considered to be non-living as they lack the ability to carry out metabolic functions and reproduce on their own; they are non-cellular. - Viruses are highly specific, targeting specific host cells based on the interaction between viral proteins and host receptors. - Viruses can infect a wide range of organisms, including plants, animals, and even bacteria (known as bacteriophages). - Viral infections can cause a wide range of diseases in their hosts, from mild illnesses to severe infections. - Viruses can be transmitted through various routes such as respiratory droplets, bodily fluids, contaminated surfaces, or through insect vectors. - Some viruses may have spikes to help attach to the host cell. - Vaccines and antiviral medicines have been developed to prevent and treat viral infections, but their use varies depending on the specific virus.

subjective.question: Write the unique properties of viruses.
subjective.answer: - Living as well as nonliving characteristics - Unable to cultivate in laboratory easily - Simplest structure - Complex interaction with host

subjective.question: Describe the virus particle (virion) — capsid shapes and types of virions.
subjective.answer: The virus particle is called a virion and consists of nucleic acid surrounded by a protein coat (capsid). Capsid shapes: isometric, helical and complex. Two types of virions: naked (without envelope) and enveloped (surrounded by a lipid membrane).

subjective.question: What is a genome?
subjective.answer: A genome is the complete set of genetic information in an organism. It provides all of the information the organism requires to function. In living organisms, the genome is stored in long molecules of DNA called chromosomes.

subjective.question: What is a gene?
subjective.answer: A gene is a segment of DNA molecule that encodes for the synthesis of a single polypeptide.

subjective.question: Write two names of acellular particles.
subjective.answer: Viroids, virusoids, and prions.

subjective.question: What is “life”?
subjective.answer: Life is a complex set of processes resulting from the actions of proteins specified by nucleic acids. (The nucleic acids of living things are in action all the time.)

subjective.question: Why do viruses need a host?
subjective.answer: - No enzymes of their own - No metabolism - Require host machinery

subjective.question: What is the composition of the capsid?
subjective.answer: The capsid is proteinic (protein) in nature and is composed of protomers and/or capsomers.

subjective.question: Write at least 3 roles of the viral capsid.
subjective.answer: - Protection of genome - Prevent digestion by cellular enzymes - In the cytoplasm, helps to introduce the genome into the host cell - Bind to cell surface

subjective.question: Differentiate between capsid and envelope.
subjective.answer: Capsid: The capsid (coat) protein is the basic unit of structure. Virus particles contain the viral genome packaged in a protein coat called the capsid. Its functions are to: protect viral nucleic acid; interact specifically with the viral nucleic acid for packaging; interact with the vector for specific transmission; interact with host receptors for entry into the cell; allow for release of nucleic acid upon entry into a new cell; and assist in processes of viral and/or host gene regulation. Envelope: In some viruses, the capsid is covered by an envelope — a lipid bilayer, derived from the host cell membranes, that contains viral proteins (lipids, proteins and carbohydrates). Spikes are projections from the surface of the envelope by which viruses attach to host cells (e.g. the ability of influenza virus to clump red blood cells is associated with spikes). Viruses whose capsids are not covered by an envelope are known as non-enveloped viruses. The envelope is mostly host-specific, derived from the host cell membranes, and helps the virus to enter the host.

subjective.question: Compare the symmetrical properties of the kinds of viral symmetry.
subjective.answer: Symmetry refers to the way in which capsomere units are arranged in the viral capsid. Two kinds of symmetry are known in viruses, which relate to the two primary shapes, i.e. rod and spherical shape of virus. Rod-shaped viruses have helical symmetry and spherical-shaped viruses have icosahedral symmetry.

subjective.question: What is the Baltimore classification? Give its classes.
subjective.answer: The Baltimore classification system, developed in the 1970s (1971) by Nobel laureate David Baltimore, categorizes viruses based on the type of nucleic acid genome and the replication strategy of the virus. Its seven classes are: - Class I: double-stranded DNA viruses (e.g. Adeno, Herpes) - Class II: single-stranded DNA viruses (e.g. Parvo) - Class III: double-stranded RNA viruses (e.g. Reo) - Class IV: positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses (e.g. Polio, Picorna) - Class V: negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses (e.g. Ortho) - Class VI: single-stranded RNA viruses that reverse transcribe (Retro) - Class VII: double-stranded DNA viruses that reverse transcribe (Hepadna)

subjective.question: What is the host range of a virus? Discuss it.
subjective.answer: - Host range refers to the spectrum of host cells that the virus can infect — the spectrum of host cells in which a virus can multiply. - Most viruses infect only specific types of cells in one host species. - Host range is determined by the specific attachment site on the host cell's surface and the availability of host cellular factors. - Most viruses are host specific and bind to specific receptors on cells; in animal viruses, receptors on the plasma membrane form hydrogen bonds with the viral surface. - Viruses that infect bacteria are called bacteriophages, or phages. - Viral host range includes: plants, vertebrates, invertebrates, protists, bacteria and fungi.

subjective.question: Define viral tropism of cells and tissues, with an example.
subjective.answer: In a general sense, viral tropism refers to the ability of a given virus to productively infect a particular cell (cellular tropism), tissue (tissue tropism) or host species (host tropism). For example, if a particular virus can productively infect rabbits but no other vertebrate hosts such as humans, that virus would be said to have a host tropism limited to rabbits. Similarly, if the same virus could productively infect rabbit macrophages but not any other rabbit cells, that virus would be said to have a cellular tropism limited to macrophages.

subjective.question: What are the theories of the origin / evolution of viruses? (3–5 marks)
subjective.answer: - First theory: They may have originated and evolved with the other life forms. - Second theory: They may have arisen from segments of the cellular nucleic acids which acquired the ability to replicate at the expense of the host cell. - Third theory (Regressive theory): Viruses arose from free-living organisms which gradually lost genetic information, until they became totally dependent on the biosynthetic pathways of their host cells.

subjective.topic: Viral Replication & Effects on the Host Cell
subjective.question: Write the steps of the animal virus infection (life) cycle.
subjective.answer: Viral replication involves six steps: attachment, penetration, uncoating, replication (gene expression), assembly and release. - During attachment and penetration, the virus attaches itself to a host cell and injects its genetic material into it. - During uncoating, replication, and assembly, the viral DNA or RNA incorporates itself into the host cell's genetic material and induces it to replicate the viral genome. - During release, the newly created viruses are released from the host cell, either by causing the cell to break apart, waiting for the cell to die, or by budding off through the cell membrane.

subjective.topic: Viral Replication & Effects on the Host Cell
subjective.question: Describe the mechanism of viral attack (entry) on the host cell.
subjective.answer: Viral entry pathways: A virus can fuse either directly with the plasma membrane (receptor-mediated fusion) or after being swallowed into an endosome. Which of these routes is followed depends on the type of virus. In fusion with the plasma membrane, the virus binds to a protein in the cell membrane; the function of this cellular protein (a receptor for the virus) is perverted to induce a conformational change in the viral fusion protein, leading to fusion. For a virus that is triggered within an endosome, the endosome's acidic conditions induce fusion. In either case, the viral genome passes through a fusion pore into the cytosol, and infection is initiated.

subjective.topic: Viral Replication & Effects on the Host Cell
subjective.question: Describe uncoating of viruses.
subjective.answer: During virus entry, capsid shells are primed and disassembled in a complex, tightly regulated, multi-step process termed uncoating. - Uncoating means removal of the capsid from the virus. - It exposes the viral genome in the host cell (in the cytoplasm, with the help of cellular enzymes); the protein coat around the genome gets disintegrated. - It is a vital, important step: it makes the genome ready to take over the host machinery and activates the cascade of steps required for viral replication.

subjective.topic: Viral Replication & Effects on the Host Cell
subjective.question: What are the effects of an attack of viruses on host cells? (2–3 marks)
subjective.answer: When viruses attack host cells, they replicate inside the host to produce new viral particles and use the host's metabolism, which can damage or destroy the host cell. The process can trigger host defence mechanisms that may cause tissue damage, contributing to the symptoms of the disease. Consequently, the damage can cause pathological effects, which could result in inflammation, tissue damage, cell death, and organ dysfunction, having grave implications for the host's health. Possible effects of the viral genome on the host cell are: - Genetic alterations - Physical damage - Oncogenesis

subjective.topic: Viral Replication & Effects on the Host Cell
subjective.question: What is the role of proteins and glycoproteins in the life cycle of a virus?
subjective.answer: Proteins and glycoproteins have essential roles in the life cycle of viruses. They facilitate the attachment and recognition of host cells, assist in the penetration of the viral genome into the host cell, and interact with the host cell machinery to initiate the replication and transcription of viral genomes. Furthermore, the assembly of new viral particles, genome packaging, and release of new viral particles is also reliant on viral proteins and glycoproteins. Proteins and glycoproteins are involved at every stage of the viral life cycle, playing crucial roles in the process.

subjective.question: What is a bacteriophage? Explain the lytic and lysogenic cycles.
subjective.answer: A bacteriophage, also known informally as a phage, is a virus that infects and replicates within bacteria and archaea. Lytic cycle: The phages take over the machinery of the cell to make phage components. They then destroy, or lyse, the cell, releasing new phage particles. Lysogenic cycle: The phage infects a bacterium and inserts its DNA into the bacterial chromosome, allowing the phage DNA (now called a prophage) to be copied and passed on along with the cell's own DNA; lysogenic phages incorporate their nucleic acids into the chromosome of the host cell and replicate with it as a unit without destroying the cell.

subjective.question: Describe the method to grow bacteriophage.
subjective.answer: Two methods: - In liquid media - On solid media

subjective.question: What are T phages?
subjective.answer: - Head and tail, called binal symmetry - Icosahedral head and helical tail symmetry

subjective.question: Describe the replication of T-phages.
subjective.answer: Replication stages: 1. Attachment, 2. Penetration, 3. Uncoating, 4. Biosynthesis, 5. Release. Attachment: To specific receptors — teichoic acid, lipids, proteins, flagella — on specific bacterial hosts. Penetration: The capsid is left outside. Biosynthesis: Bacterial ribosomes translate viral proteins; proteins modify bacterial RNA polymerase; proteins for new virions are made. Assembly: In T4, helper proteins are required; base plates are assembled first, tails are built afterwards, heads are constructed separately; the whole process takes about 15 minutes. Release: By lysis (tailed phages, using endolysin), extrusion (enveloped), budding, or secretion.

subjective.question: Describe the M13 phage.
subjective.answer: - Simple genome - 6.4 kb - Single stranded - Positive sense - Circular DNA encoding ten genes - Icosahedral symmetry - Capsid can be expanded by protein subunits - Hence, genomic size can also be increased

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: What is viral recombination? Also define intramolecular recombination.
subjective.answer: Viral recombination: The exchange or transfer of genetic material between different but closely related viruses infecting the same cell. It can also occur between virus and host; recombinants contain new genetic information. Intramolecular recombination: Usually in DNA viruses — dissociation and re-establishment of covalent bonds within nucleic acids, by a template-switching mechanism.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: What is complementation? Also write its types.
subjective.answer: Complementation is the assignment of mutants to functional groups resulting in production of one or both parent viruses. One of the viruses provides a functional gene product, which allows functional analysis of unknown mutations. Types of complementation: - Allelic (intragenic) complementation: different mutants have defects in the same protein. - Non-allelic (intergenic) complementation: results from mutants with defects in different genes.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: What is suppression of a viral genome? How is viral suppression done / define informational suppression.
subjective.answer: Suppression of a viral genome is the inhibition of a mutant phenotype by a second suppressor mutation, which may be either in the viral genome or in the host cell. Informational suppression: The mechanism is different from the suppression of chain-terminating amber mutations by host-encoded suppressor tRNAs, which is also referred to as informational suppression.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Write down the ways of reversion.
subjective.answer: Mutant viruses can revert by three ways: - True reversion: Back mutation of the original mutation; gives the wild-type genotype or phenotype. - Intragenic reversion: A compensatory mutation, which occurs in the same originally mutated gene, restoring it. - Extragenic reversion: A suppressor mutation in a different gene — a virus gene or a host gene.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Define genetic reactivation.
subjective.answer: Genetic reactivation is the production of infectious progeny from parents in which one or both are non-infectious, in a mixed infection of the cell.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Define the following terms: mutation, pseudotype, recombinant, codon, anti-codon, ribosomes, plasmid, transcription, translation.
subjective.answer: - Mutation: A permanent inheritable change in a single gene that results in the existence of two or more alleles occurring at the same locus. - Pseudotype: The viruses that have acquired the genotype of one parent and the phenotype of another. - Recombinant: A new combination of genes not found together on the chromosome in either parent; a recombinant results from crossing over. - Codon: A sequence of three bases in DNA or RNA that codes for a single amino acid; it enables specific proteins to be made by specific genes. - Anti-codon: A sequence of three bases in tRNA that is complementary to a codon in mRNA; it enables tRNA to sequence amino acids in the order specified by mRNA. - Ribosomes: Complexes of rRNA and protein in the cytoplasm that serve as platforms for translation of mRNA into protein. - Plasmid: Extrachromosomal circular DNA in bacteria, which replicates independently and encodes a product. - Transcription: Synthesis of single-stranded RNA by RNA polymerase using DNA as a template; the process in the nucleus whereby DNA is transcribed into mRNA. - Translation: The process of translating the codon sequence in mRNA into polypeptides with the help of tRNA and ribosomes.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Define the terms strain, type, variant and mutant. What is a mutant?
subjective.answer: - Strain: Lines or isolates of the same virus. - Type: Serotypes of the same virus. - Variant: A virus whose phenotype varies from the original virus. - Mutant: A virus showing genetic alteration. A mutant is an organism or a new genetic character arising or resulting from an instance of mutation, which is generally an alteration of the DNA/RNA sequence of the genome or chromosome of an organism.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Write down the types of mutant viruses.
subjective.answer: - Biochemical markers - Deletions - Host range - Non-sense - Plaque morphology - Temperature sensitive - Cold sensitive - Revertants

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Name two types of mutations that can be induced. Write the mutagen of each category.
subjective.answer: In-vitro: The nucleic acids are chemically modified; replication is not required. E.g. nitrous acid, hydroxylamine, and alkylating agents like nitrosoguanidine. In-vivo: Requires metabolically active nucleic acid that is replicating; compounds are incorporated into newly synthesized nucleic acids. E.g. 5-bromouracil (resulting in erroneous base pairing), intercalating bases that stack between bases, and UV irradiation.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: What is in-vitro mutagenesis?
subjective.answer: Another use of cloned DNA is in-vitro mutagenesis, in which a mutation is produced in a segment of cloned DNA. The DNA is then inserted into a cell or organism, and the effects of the mutation are studied. Mutations are useful to geneticists in enabling them to investigate the components of any biological process.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Mutation: good or bad?
subjective.answer: Sometimes good for the virus, as it helps it escape the immune system; but some mutations may be deleterious due to production of defective particles.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Do RNA viruses have proof-reading?
subjective.answer: Yes — yet they show higher rates of mutation than DNA viruses. (Source answer, kept as given.)

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: What is the reason behind spontaneous mutations?
subjective.answer: Spontaneous mutations arise naturally during replication. The mechanism of genome replication is the reason: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase shows a higher error rate than DNA-dependent DNA polymerase.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: What is heterozygosis?
subjective.answer: Heterozygosis is the aberrant packaging of multiple genomes. It may result in multiploidy particles and adds to the genetic complexity of the population.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: When does genetic interaction occur between viruses?
subjective.answer: Genetic interaction occurs naturally between viruses. It occurs when there is more than one infection in a host (i.e. when more than one virus infects the same host cell).

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Differentiate between RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
subjective.answer: - RNA-dependent RNA polymerase produces a single-stranded negative strand of RNA, and then it produces the positive strand of RNA. Examples: Togavirus, Picornavirus, etc. It does not require a primer and lacks exonuclease (proof-reading) activity. - DNA-dependent RNA polymerase produces single-stranded positive RNA genomes (mRNA) from a DNA template (transcription). Examples: HIV-1, HIV-2, HTLV-1.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: What is the difference between introns and exons?
subjective.answer: - Intron: Non-coding regions on the viral genome. - Exon: The coding region on the viral genome.

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: Define transposons. Also write their types and properties.
subjective.answer: A transposon is a sequence of DNA that can change its position, from place to place within a genome. Types of transposons (two groups): - Simple transposons: In prokaryotes, which do not undergo reverse transcription. E.g. genome of Enterobacteria phage Mu. - Retro transposons: Closely resemble the retroviral genome; bound by long repeat units (LTRs); move by means of a transcription / reverse transcription / integration mechanism; found in eukaryotes. E.g. in Metaviridae and Pseudoviridae. Properties: - Responsible for high mutation - Promote genetic rearrangements like deletion, inversion, duplication, etc. - Often accompanied by replication - Control their own transposition functions

subjective.topic: Viral Genetics — Mutation, Recombination, Reversion & Suppression
subjective.question: What is reverse transcriptase / reverse transcription?
subjective.answer: Reverse transcription is a process in which double-stranded DNA molecules are made from a single-stranded RNA. The name of this method originated from its opposite direction to the transcription process. It involves the presence of: reverse transcriptase (an enzyme), a primer (some bases of nucleotide segments), and reverse transcriptase inhibitor leucine-rich repeat protein.

subjective.question: Name the in-vitro genetic techniques used in virology. Also give the in-vivo / molecular and phenotypic analysis techniques.
subjective.answer: In-vitro techniques: - Physical analysis - Isolation of nucleic acids from virus preparations - Direct analysis of DNA using restriction endonuclease enzymes - Use of vectors in DNA sequencing - Electron microscopy - RNA sequence analysis using reverse transcriptase In-vivo (viral genotype and phenotype) — Molecular analysis: - Molecular cloning - Gel electrophoresis - Hybridization of complementary nucleotide sequences Phenotypic analysis: - Cell-free extracts to translate mRNAs - Transfection tests - In-vitro protein formation - In-vivo protein replication Phylogenetic analysis is also a standard technique in virology. In short, the genetic techniques used in virology are in-vitro analysis (physical analysis) and in-vivo analysis (virus genotype and phenotype analysis).

subjective.question: What is fluorescence? State the principle of the fluorescence microscope.
subjective.answer: Fluorescence is the ability of substances to absorb short wavelengths of light (ultraviolet) and give off light at a longer wavelength (visible). Principle of the fluorescence microscope: The specimen is illuminated with light of a specific wavelength, which is absorbed by the fluorophores, causing them to emit light of longer wavelengths. Fluorescent dyes are used for specimen staining; examples of fluorescent stains are DAPI and Hoechst.

subjective.question: Phase-contrast microscope: principle and applications.
subjective.answer: Phase-contrast microscopy (PCM) is an optical microscopy technique that converts phase shifts in light passing through a transparent specimen into brightness changes in the image. Phase shifts themselves are invisible, but become visible when shown as brightness variations. Principle: When light passes through cells, small phase shifts occur. These phase shifts are converted into changes in amplitude, which can be observed as differences in image contrast. Applications: cell culture; live cell imaging — living cells can be observed in their natural state without previous fixation or labelling.

subjective.question: What is differential interference contrast (DIC / Nomarski) microscopy?
subjective.answer: DIC, also known as Nomarski interference contrast microscopy, is used to enhance the contrast in unstained, transparent samples. DIC works on the principle of interferometry to gain information about the optical path length. It is a more expensive, label-free microscopy technique with high sensitivity to thin cellular material, even when it is located within thick tissue. It is useful for rendering contrast in transparent samples and gives brilliant pseudo-3D relief shading images. (In the Spring 2022 paper, a DIC/Nomarski microscope was the answer for viewing transparent samples.)

subjective.question: Differentiate between scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
subjective.answer: SEM: An electron gun produces a finely focused beam of electrons called the primary electron beam. These electrons pass through electromagnetic lenses and are directed over the surface of the specimen. The primary electron beam knocks electrons out of the surface of the specimen, and the secondary electrons thus produced are transmitted to an electron collector, amplified, and used to produce an image on a viewing screen or photographic plate. The image is called a scanning electron micrograph. TEM: A focused beam of electrons from an electron gun passes through the ultrathin section of the specimen. The beam is focused on a small area of the specimen by an electromagnetic condenser lens. Instead of being placed on a glass slide, the specimen is usually placed on a copper mesh grid.

subjective.question: What is scanned probe microscopy? Write its principle, types and limitations.
subjective.answer: Scanned probe microscopy forms images of surfaces using a physical probe that scans the specimen; it was founded in 1981. Principle: The interaction between the sharp probe and the surface provides a 3D topographic image of the surface at the atomic scale. The two most popular modes (types) are: - Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy (STM): measures the electrical current between the tip and the specimen. - Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM): measures the electrostatic force between the tip and the specimen. Image formation: The tip is scanned over the surface, a value is recorded, and it is displayed as a heat map. Limitations: The detailed shape of the probe is difficult to determine sometimes; slower in acquiring images; the maximum image size is smaller; cannot examine buried solid–solid or liquid–liquid interfaces.

subjective.question: Which dyes are used in TEM?
subjective.answer: Uranyl acetate, lead citrate, and osmium tetroxide are commonly used dyes in Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to enhance contrast and visualize biological specimens. Contrast can be greatly enhanced by using a “dye” that absorbs electrons and produces a darker image in the stained region — lead citrate, osmium tetroxide, tungsten, uranyl acetate and uranium (stains). These metals can be fixed onto the specimen (positive staining) or used to increase the electron opacity of the surrounding field (negative staining).

subjective.question: Write two limitations of the electron microscope.
subjective.answer: Only a very thin section of a specimen (about 100 nm) can be studied effectively. Specimens must be fixed, dehydrated, and viewed under a high vacuum to prevent electron scattering. These treatments not only kill the specimen, but also cause shrinkage and distortion.

subjective.question: What is the function of the condenser in a light microscope?
subjective.answer: The function of the condenser is to focus the light rays onto the specimen under observation.

subjective.question: Name 3 monochromatic light sources used in microscopy.
subjective.answer: - Xenon arc lamps - Mercury vapor lamps - Super-continuum source - High power LED

subjective.topic: Cultivation of Viruses — Cell Culture, Eggs & Isolation
subjective.question: What is cell culture?
subjective.answer: Cell culture is the process by which cells are grown under controlled conditions, generally outside their natural environment; in practice it refers to the culturing of cells derived from animal cells. Cell culture was first successfully undertaken by Ross Harrison in 1907. After the cells of interest have been isolated from living tissue, they can subsequently be maintained under carefully controlled conditions.

subjective.topic: Cultivation of Viruses — Cell Culture, Eggs & Isolation
subjective.question: How many types of tissue culture are there?
subjective.answer: There are three types of tissue culture: - Organ culture - Explant culture - Cell culture

subjective.topic: Cultivation of Viruses — Cell Culture, Eggs & Isolation
subjective.question: Write the different routes of inoculation in the embryonated egg (animal cells). (2–5 marks)
subjective.answer: Following are the routes for inoculation: - Chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) inoculation — the chicken embryo at about day 4 post-fertilization has a highly vascularized chorioallantoic membrane that expands from the hind-gut - Amniotic inoculation - Allantoic inoculation - Yolk sac inoculation — the yolk sac membrane (YSM) is also highly vascularized

subjective.topic: Cultivation of Viruses — Cell Culture, Eggs & Isolation
subjective.question: Describe embryonic inoculation (I/E, I/C and I/V inoculation).
subjective.answer: Embryos are inoculated and incubated for a period of one to six days, during which they are observed twice a day for evidence of death of the embryo. Some viruses, such as equine encephalomyelitis virus, kill the embryo within 24 hours, while others kill the embryos in 2 to 3 days. Some viruses readily multiply within the embryonic tissue and are seldom lethal. Embryo death is accompanied by collapse of the large blood vessels of the chorioallantois, so that they are difficult to see upon candling the egg, whereas they are quite distinct while the embryos are alive. Normal movements of the embryo are no longer observed if the embryo is moribund or dead. If the embryo is not dead after 5 or 6 days of incubation, it is killed or examined for lesions. These inoculations of embryos are not widely used.

subjective.topic: Cultivation of Viruses — Cell Culture, Eggs & Isolation
subjective.question: Which type of centrifuge is best for the isolation of viruses?
subjective.answer: Ultracentrifuge. Ultracentrifuges are typically considered to be the best type of centrifuge for virus isolation, as they have the capability to separate viral particles from other contaminants at high speed and with high precision. These centrifuges typically operate at speeds of up to 100,000 rotations per minute (rpm) and have capacities ranging from a few millilitres to several litres. Additionally, ultracentrifuges are capable of separating individual viral particles based on differences in size, density, and buoyant density, which can be important for the purification of virus particles from complex biological mixtures. Thus, ultracentrifuges are widely accepted as the gold standard for virus isolation and purification.

subjective.topic: Cultivation of Viruses — Cell Culture, Eggs & Isolation
subjective.question: Define “mice” as a research model.
subjective.answer: Mice are the most commonly used animal model for studying human disease, and for many good reasons: mice are biologically very similar to humans and get many of the same diseases for the same genetic reasons. Mice can be genetically manipulated to mimic virtually any human disease or condition.

subjective.question: What is the virus neutralization test? Describe it.
subjective.answer: It is a serological test that detects the presence of viral neutralizing antibodies. The antibodies bind to viral particles; these antibodies block viral infectivity and prevent viral infections. Procedure points (from the Fall 2021 / Spring 2022 solved papers): - Used to confirm the identity of an unknown viral isolate - Use of a known dilution of specific antiserum mixed with multiple dilutions of virus; a wide range of dilutions is used - Equal volumes of viral dilution and immune serum are used - Observation of the virus to produce cytopathic effects - Inoculation of 5 to 6 animals, with an equal number of controls - Observation of animals for signs, lesions or deaths

subjective.question: What is the principle of the fluorescence antibody technique (FAT)?
subjective.answer: The principle is based on the observation that virus proteins (antigen) are present in the tissues, e.g. rabies virus present in nervous tissues. The Fluorescence Antibody Technique (FAT) is based on the use of fluorescent-labelled antibodies that specifically bind to the antigen of interest. The fluorescent tag allows for the visualization of the bound antibody–antigen complex, which is detected using a fluorescence microscope. The technique is highly specific and sensitive, allowing for the rapid and accurate detection of a wide range of pathogens in biological samples.

subjective.question: What are the uses of the immunofluorescence / fluorescence antibody technique? (2–5 marks)
subjective.answer: Immunofluorescence is an important immunochemical technique that allows for the detection and localization of a wide variety of antigens in different types of tissues and various cell preparations. It can be used to visualize structures such as intermediate-sized cell filaments. It is applied on tissue sections, cultured cell lines and individual cells. - The FAT involves fluorescent-labelled antibodies that specifically bind to the antigen of interest, resulting in a fluorescent signal that can be visualized under a fluorescence microscope. - The technique can be used to detect a wide range of antigens, including viral, bacterial, fungal, and parasitic antigens, as well as tumor markers. - The technique is highly specific and sensitive, allowing detection of very low levels of pathogen antigens in biological samples. - The FAT is widely used in clinical microbiology and virology for the rapid and accurate diagnosis of infections caused by viruses and other pathogens. - In addition to diagnosis, the FAT is also used for research purposes, such as studying the localization and distribution of specific antigens within cells or tissues. - In clinical immunology and pathology, immunofluorescence is used for detection of circulating autoantibodies, detection of antigens in cells and cell membranes, detection of immune complexes in biopsy material, and detection of circulating immune cells.

subjective.question: Describe the agglutination and precipitation tests. Differentiate between them. (3–5 marks)
subjective.answer: Agglutination is the process of clumping of antigens with their respective antibodies. Precipitation is a process where soluble antigens bind with their specific antibody at an optimum temperature and pH, resulting in the formation of an insoluble precipitate. Principle: Viruses may be sensitized by specific antibody. In the presence of electrolyte, the virus particles cling to each other, forming aggregates, observed through microscopic or macroscopic examination. Antigen preparation: centrifugation; washing in buffered solution; re-centrifugation. Applications (two ways): 1. If the virus is known, antibodies can be detected. 2. If known serum is available, an unknown virus can be detected.

subjective.question: What is the complement fixation test (CFT)?
subjective.answer: The complement fixation test is an immunological test used to detect the presence of either specific antibody or specific antigen on the basis of complement fixation. Complement is a system of serum proteins that react with antigen–antibody complexes; if this reaction occurs on a cell surface, it will result in the formation of trans-membrane pores and therefore destruction of the cell. Short procedure: Serum is separated from the patient. Patients naturally have different levels of complement proteins in their serum, so the complement proteins in the patient's serum are first destroyed (by heating, which destroys complement but none of the antibodies) and replaced by a known amount of standardized complement proteins (frequently obtained from guinea pig serum). The antigen of interest is added to the serum. Then sheep red blood cells (sRBCs) which have been pre-bound to anti-sRBC antibodies are added. Result interpretation: If the patient's serum contains antibodies against the antigen of interest, they bind to the antigen to form antigen–antibody complexes, and the complement proteins react with these complexes and are depleted; thus, when the sRBC–antibody complexes are added, no complement is left and there is no lysis. If no antibodies against the antigen of interest are present, the complement is not depleted and it reacts with the sRBC–antibody complexes, lysing the sRBCs and spilling their contents into the solution, turning the solution pink.

subjective.question: Which techniques are used for the detection of the viral genome in cells?
subjective.answer: Classical techniques: - Complement fixation tests (CFT) - Haemagglutination inhibition tests - Immunofluorescence techniques (IF) - Neutralization tests (viral & serum) - Single radial haemolysis Newer techniques: - Radioimmunoassay (RIA) - Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (EIA) - Particle agglutination - Western blot (WB) - Recombinant immunoblot assay (RIBA)

subjective.topic: Latency, Pathogenesis & Effects of Physical/Chemical Factors
subjective.question: What are latent (occult) infections of viruses? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Some viruses reappear to cause acute disease; the pathogenic viruses having the ability to lie dormant (or latent) within the host cell are in the lysogenic part of the life cycle. They are enveloped viruses (e.g. paramyxoviruses, retroviruses, arenavirus), cause no disruption of cellular functions, and promote shedding of viral antigens from the cell surface. Three examples: HSV, Adenovirus, SSPE. - HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus): Primary infection in early age; found only during recurrent acute episodes; virus can be isolated from tissue homogenates. - Adenovirus: Self-limiting; persistent infection of tonsils and adenoids; failure in viral isolation; absence of mature virion; DNA in linear episomal form. - Measles virus: Incomplete viral production; immature nucleocapsids produced; disease depends on immune response; may cause tumorigenesis.

subjective.topic: Latency, Pathogenesis & Effects of Physical/Chemical Factors
subjective.question: Define latency and the lysogenic part of the life cycle. Write about episomal and proviral latency, and the types of latent viral infections.
subjective.answer: The pathogenic viruses having the ability to lie dormant (or latent) within the host cell are in the lysogenic part of the life cycle. Latency is the phase in which viral proliferation ceases after initial infection, but the viral genome is not fully eradicated. Episomal latency: Use of genetic episomes; viral genes float in the cytoplasm or nucleus; more vulnerable to the host immune system. Examples: chicken pox and herpes simplex viruses. Proviral latency: The virus genome is integrated into the DNA of a host cell; automatic host cell division occurs during viral replication; the viral genome enters the nucleus. Example: HIV. Maintaining latency: For continuity of infection, by genes expressed during latency, to evade the host immune system and to protect the virus genome from being digested by cellular enzymes. Types of latent viral infections: chronic persistent infections and latent occult viral infections.

subjective.topic: Latency, Pathogenesis & Effects of Physical/Chemical Factors
subjective.question: What are the types of pathogenesis in the interaction of virus and host cells?
subjective.answer: - Inapparent - Apparent - Acute - Subacute - Chronic - Latency

subjective.topic: Latency, Pathogenesis & Effects of Physical/Chemical Factors
subjective.question: What are the effects of physical and chemical factors on viruses?
subjective.answer: Inactivation of a virus represents permanent loss of infectivity (contamination). - Temperature: Viruses are stable at low temperature (keeping); viruses with an envelope are heat sensitive. - Drying: Most of the viruses are sensitive to drying. - Irradiation (UV, X-ray): Inactivation of viruses. - Chemical agents: Organic solvents (chloroform) inactivate viruses with an envelope; oxido-reductant agents (formaldehyde, chlorine, iodine) cause inactivation. - pH: At low pH, viruses without an envelope are mostly stable.

subjective.topic: Latency, Pathogenesis & Effects of Physical/Chemical Factors
subjective.question: Describe the mechanism of enzyme action.
subjective.answer: Enzymes work by binding with specific substrates to form enzyme–substrate complexes. This binding process lowers the activation energy required for the reaction to take place. Enzymes may increase reaction rates by weakening bonds or providing reactive groups and surfaces that enhance the chemical interaction between substrates. The reaction is then facilitated and product formation is accelerated. Once the reaction is complete, the product is released from the enzyme, which can then be used again to catalyse further reactions. This repetitive use by enzymes makes the process highly efficient, specific, and essential for various biological processes.

subjective.question: What is paramyxo? (2–3 marks)
subjective.answer: Para means “beyond” and myxo means “mucus”. Paramyxo and orthomyxo were formerly known as myxoviruses.

subjective.question: What are the functions of the different proteins of Paramyxoviridae?
subjective.answer: - N – The nucleocapsid protein associates with genomic RNA and protects the RNA from nuclease digestion. - P – The phosphoprotein binds to the N and L proteins and forms part of the RNA polymerase complex. - M – The matrix protein assembles between the envelope and the nucleocapsid core; it organizes and maintains virion structure. - F – The fusion protein projects from the envelope surface as a trimer and mediates entry. - H/HN/G – The cell attachment proteins span the viral envelope and project from the surface as spikes. - L – The large protein is the catalytic subunit of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). Accessory proteins – a mechanism known as RNA editing allows multiple proteins to be produced from the P gene.

subjective.question: Write the proteins and glycoproteins encoded by orthomyxovirus (Orthomyxoviridae proteins).
subjective.answer: - Hemagglutinin (HA): A surface glycoprotein responsible for virus attachment and entry into host cells. - Neuraminidase (NA): A surface glycoprotein that cuts (cleaves) sialic acid from host-cell membranes, helping the release of new virions from infected cells and the spread of the virus throughout an infected host. - Matrix protein (M1): A protein that links the viral envelope (lipid bilayer) to the viral ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) and mediates viral assembly and budding. - Nucleoprotein (NP): A protein that complexes with viral RNA to form the viral RNPs responsible for viral genome replication and transcription. - RNA polymerase: A trimeric complex composed of three viral proteins (PB1, PB2, and PA) that catalyze viral RNA synthesis (replication and transcription) in the host cell nucleus.

subjective.question: What are RNPs (ribonucleoproteins)?
subjective.answer: The segmented genome is encapsidated with each segment in a separate nucleocapsid, called ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNPs). Terminal sequences of RNA are bound to the trimeric RdRp, and all these RNPs are surrounded by one envelope. In general, a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) is a complex of ribonucleic acid and RNA-binding protein. These complexes play an integral part in a number of important biological functions, including transcription, translation, regulating gene expression and regulating the metabolism of RNA. Examples of RNPs include the ribosome, the enzyme telomerase, vault ribonucleoproteins, RNase P, hnRNP and small nuclear RNPs (snRNPs).

subjective.question: What is the genome of the togavirus? (Genomic properties of Togavirus.)
subjective.answer: - Linear, non-segmented, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA - 10,000–12,000 nucleotides - The virus is enveloped and forms spherical particles (65–70 nm diameter) - The capsid is icosahedral, constructed of 240 monomers, having a triangulation number of 4

subjective.question: Write down the steps involved in the replication of the togavirus. (3–5 marks)
subjective.answer: - Entry into the host cell is achieved by attachment of the viral E glycoprotein to host receptors, which mediates clathrin-mediated endocytosis. - The receptors for binding are unknown; glycoprotein petal-like spikes act as attachment proteins. - After virus attachment and entry into the cell, gene expression and replication take place within the cytoplasm. - In genome replication, the viral RNA acts as both genome and mRNA; after fusion of the viral capsid with the cell receptor, the RNA is released into the cytoplasm.

subjective.question: Describe the coronavirus (structure, taxonomy and diseases).
subjective.answer: Coronaviruses are found in avian and mammalian species. They resemble each other in morphology and chemical structure: for example, the coronaviruses of humans and cattle are antigenically related. In animals, various coronaviruses enter many different tissues and cause a variety of diseases, but in humans they are only proved to cause mild upper respiratory infections, i.e. common colds. On rare occasions, gastrointestinal coronavirus infection has been associated. Structure: Spherical or pleomorphic enveloped particles containing single-stranded (positive-sense) RNA associated with a nucleoprotein within a capsid comprised of matrix protein. The envelope bears club-shaped glycoprotein projections. The genomic size of coronaviruses ranges from approximately 26 to 32 kb, the largest for an RNA virus. Taxonomy: Order Nidovirales; Family Coronaviridae; Subfamily Coronavirinae. Diseases: Common cold (second most common cause of the common cold); SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome); GI tract infections in kids.

subjective.question: Explain the replication cycle of coronavirus.
subjective.answer: - Attachment of the viral S-protein to receptors - Endocytosis of the virus into the host cell - Fusion of the virus membrane with the endosomal membrane - Genome is released into the cytoplasm - Synthesis and proteolytic cleavage of the replicase polyprotein - A dsRNA genome is synthesized from the genomic ssRNA(+) - The dsRNA genome is transcribed, providing viral mRNAs / new ssRNA(+) genomes - Synthesis of structural proteins encoded by sub-genomic mRNAs - Assembly and budding at membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the intermediate compartments, and/or the Golgi complex - Release of new virions by exocytosis

subjective.question: What are the different segments of the Bunyavirus genome, in terms of the proteins they encode?
subjective.answer: Bunyavirus genomes consist of three RNA segments called large, medium, and small (L, M, and S, respectively) that encode four structural proteins (the RNA polymerase or L protein; two glycoproteins, Gn and Gc; and the nucleocapsid protein, N), as well as one or two nonstructural proteins (NSm and NSs).

subjective.question: Describe Bunyavirus — structure, classification and clinical manifestations.
subjective.answer: Structure: Bunyaviruses are spherical, enveloped particles 90 to 100 nm in diameter. They contain three segments of antisense (and sometimes ambisense) single-stranded RNA combined with nucleoprotein. Two external glycoproteins form surface projections. Classification and antigenic types: Bunyaviridae is the largest family, of 5 genera: 1. Orthobunyavirus, 2. Hantavirus, 3. Nairovirus, 4. Phlebovirus, 5. Tospovirus. Clinical manifestations: Bunyaviruses cause fevers, sometimes with rash. In addition, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus may cause hemorrhage; Rift Valley fever virus may cause hemorrhagic hepatitis, encephalitis, or blindness.

subjective.question: Name diseases caused by Peribunyaviridae, and name 4 viruses of the family Peribunyaviridae.
subjective.answer: Diseases caused by Peribunyaviridae: - Rift Valley fever - La Crosse encephalitis - California encephalitis Viruses of family Peribunyaviridae: - California encephalitis virus - La Crosse encephalitis virus - Jamestown Canyon virus - Snowshoe hare virus

subjective.question: Define retrovirus.
subjective.answer: Retroviruses are the only animal viruses that integrate into the host cell's genome. The retroviral genomes can accommodate changes to their configuration. The retroviral life cycle begins in the nucleus of an infected cell.

subjective.question: Write the genome structure / genomic properties of retroviruses.
subjective.answer: Genome of retrovirus: - Single-stranded RNA viruses - Positive sense - Enveloped - Changes to DNA by the RT enzyme There are three important genes: 1. GAG, 2. ENV, 3. POL. Structure of retroviruses: It is a single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus, icosahedral in shape. All retroviruses are surrounded by a viral envelope. It contains two identical RNA molecules and reverse transcriptase enzymes.

subjective.question: What is the genetic makeup of a retrovirus? (Gag, Pol, Env.) (5–10 marks)
subjective.answer: The retrovirus has a diploid nature. There are 3 very important genes: GAG: The gag gene makes protein p24, which serves as the capsule (capsid) around the RNA and is cone-shaped; the gag gene gives the capsid protein. ENV: Envelope glycoproteins (gp41 and gp120). Gp41 is the transmembrane protein; gp120 is the outer glycoprotein and binds the host receptor. The env gene gives the molecules of the envelope protein. POL: Reverse transcriptase polymerase, with integrase activity; it makes DNA from RNA. The pol gene gives molecules of reverse transcriptase.

subjective.question: Describe the replication of retroviruses.
subjective.answer: Once inside the host cell cytoplasm, the virus uses its own reverse transcriptase (RT) enzyme to produce DNA from its RNA genome — the reverse of the usual pattern, thus “retro” (backwards). The new DNA is then incorporated into the host cell genome by an integrase enzyme; in this integrated state the virus is referred to as a provirus. The host cell then treats the viral DNA as part of its own genome, transcribing and translating the viral genes along with the cell's own genes, and the proteins produced are required to assemble new copies of the virus. It is difficult to detect the virus until it has infected the host; infection will persist indefinitely. Early steps: Retroviral particles must bind specifically to their target cells (infection requires that the cell have a surface protein that can serve as a receptor for the envelope protein of the retrovirus), cross the plasma membrane, reverse-transcribe their RNA genome, uncoat the cores, find their way to the nuclear membrane, penetrate into the nucleus and hijack the cellular machinery. When a retrovirus infects a cell, its molecules of reverse transcriptase are carried into the cell attached to the viral RNA molecules; the reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA copies of the RNA, and this dsDNA is integrated into the host chromosome with the help of the viral enzyme integrase. Later stages: Transcription, translation (the inserts are transcribed by the host's enzymes into fresh RNA molecules, which re-enter the cytosol, where some are translated by host ribosomes), assembly, maturation, budding and release.

subjective.question: Write the subfamilies of Herpesviridae (Herpesvirinae).
subjective.answer: Alphaherpesvirinae: Herpes Simplex Virus group; latent infections in sensory ganglia; genome size 120–180 kbp. Members: Simplexvirus, Varicellovirus, Human herpesvirus-I and II, Human herpesvirus-III. Betaherpesvirinae: Cytomegalovirus group; restricted host range; genome size 140–253 kbp. Members: Cytomegalovirus, Muromegalovirus, Roseolovirus, Human herpesvirus-V, Mouse cytomegalovirus-I, Human herpesvirus-VI and VII. Gammaherpesvirinae: Lymphoproliferative virus group; infection of lymphoblastic cells; genome size 105–175 kbp. Members: Lymphocryptovirus, Rhadinovirus, Human herpesvirus-IV, Human herpesvirus-VIII.

subjective.question: Write a note on herpes virus.
subjective.answer: Herpes virus is a type of virus that causes herpes infections and has DNA as its genetic material. The herpes simplex virus, also known as HSV, causes herpes. Herpes can appear in various parts of the body, most commonly on the genitals or mouth. There are two types of the herpes simplex virus: HSV-1, which primarily causes oral herpes and is generally responsible for cold sores and fever blisters around the mouth and on the face; and HSV-2, which primarily causes genital herpes and is generally responsible for genital herpes outbreaks.

subjective.question: What are the properties of picornavirus? (Viral classification of picornavirus.)
subjective.answer: The picornaviruses are small (22 to 30 nm), non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA viruses with icosahedral (cubic) symmetry. A picornavirus belongs to the family Picornaviridae and order Picornavirales; vertebrates, including humans, serve as natural hosts, and birds also serve as hosts. They are a large family of small, cytoplasmic, plus-strand RNA (~7.5 kb) viruses with a 30 nm icosahedral capsid. The virus capsid is composed of 60 protein subunits, each consisting of four polypeptides, VP1–VP4. Some species are unstable below pH 7; many are less stable at low ionic strength than at high ionic strength. Virions are insensitive to ether, chloroform, or non-ionic detergents. Viruses are inactivated by light when grown with, or in the presence of, photodynamic dyes such as neutral red or proflavin. Thermal stability varies with viruses, as does stabilization by divalent cations.

subjective.question: Name 10 plant viruses containing positive-sense RNA.
subjective.answer: - Bromoviridae - Cucumovirus - Bromovirus - Ilavirus - Alfamovirus - Ourmiavirus - Tobamovirus - Hordievirus - Pecluvirus - Furovirus - Pomovirus - Bemivirus (Also listed in the sources: Luteoviridae, Sobemovirus, Sequiviridae, Sadwavirus, Chevavirus, Tombusviridae, Tymoviridae, Comoviridae, Idaeovirus, Flexiviridae, Potyviridae, Closteroviridae.)

subjective.question: Write down the names of the negative-sense RNA plant viruses.
subjective.answer: - Bornaviridae - Bunyaviridae - Orthoviridae - Paraviridae - Rhabdoviridae

subjective.question: Write 5 families and their genera of negative-sense RNA viruses.
subjective.answer: - Bornaviridae: Bornavirus - Bunyaviridae: Bunyavirus, Hantavirus, Phlebovirus - Orthoviridae: Influenza virus A, B, C; Thogotovirus - Paraviridae (Paramyxovirinae, Pneumovirinae): Respirovirus, Morbillivirus, Rubulavirus, Pneumovirus, Metapneumovirus - Rhabdoviridae: Lyssavirus, Vesiculovirus, Ephemerovirus, Novirhabdovirus

subjective.question: Name the 3 species of Rhabdoviridae.
subjective.answer: - Rabies virus - Vesicular Stomatitis Virus - Bovine Ephemeral Fever Virus

subjective.question: Write the 5 types of arboviruses.
subjective.answer: Five viral families comprise the majority of arboviruses transmissible to humans and livestock: - Alphaviruses (Togaviridae) - Flaviviruses (Flaviviridae) - Rhabdoviruses (Rhabdoviridae) - Bunyaviruses (Bunyaviridae) - Reoviruses (Reoviridae)

subjective.question: What is the mode of transmission of arenaviruses?
subjective.answer: Arenaviruses are a family of viruses that are usually transmitted from rodents to humans. Arenaviruses are shed into the environment in the urine, saliva, or droppings of infected rodent hosts. People become infected by breathing in the virus after rodent urine, droppings or nesting materials are stirred up, such as during cleaning.

subjective.question: What are the major vectors that transmit viruses in plants?
subjective.answer: - Insect vectors (aphids, whiteflies, thrips, and leafhoppers) - Fungi - Nematodes - Mites - Environmental conditions (wind, rain, irrigation, and equipment movement)

subjective.question: Write the names of two plant viruses.
subjective.answer: - Pepper mild mottle virus - Leaf curl virus

subjective.question: Name the receptors of rabies virus and influenza virus.
subjective.answer: The acetylcholine receptor serves as a cellular receptor for rabies virus.

subjective.question: Describe the contributions of Dimitri Iwanowski and Martinus Beijerinck to the study of tobacco mosaic virus (TMV).
subjective.answer: In 1892, Dimitri Iwanowski, a Russian botanist, showed that extracts from diseased tobacco plants could transmit disease to other plants after being passed through ceramic filters fine enough to retain the smallest known bacteria. Unfortunately, he did not realize the full significance of these results. A few years later (1898), Martinus Beijerinck confirmed and extended Iwanowski's results on tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) and was the first to develop the modern idea of the virus, which he referred to as contagium vivum fluidum (“soluble living germ”); Beijerinck studied filtered diseased plant juices and found they caused disease in healthy plants.

subjective.question: What was the role of Edward Jenner in the vaccine?
subjective.answer: Edward Jenner (1796) introduced the concept of vaccination. Edward Jenner was an English physician and scientist who developed the first vaccine against smallpox. He pioneered the concept of vaccination by using cowpox virus, which was a milder form of smallpox, to confer immunity to smallpox. In 1796, he tested his theory by injecting a young boy with cowpox, and this experiment was the first successful vaccine trial in history. Jenner published his findings and started advocating for the use of cowpox vaccination to prevent smallpox, which was quickly adopted throughout Europe and the world (adopted worldwide in the 19th century). His contribution to public health is estimated to have saved millions of lives from the ravages of smallpox, and his work paved the way for the development of other vaccines. Jenner's achievement was recognized by a number of honors, including a Royal Society medal, a gold medal from Napoleon, and a knighthood from King George IV. He used cowpox against smallpox, with no knowledge of viral particles at the time.

subjective.question: What is the risk of viruses in transplantation (xenotransplantation)?
subjective.answer: (Asked in the source as “Factor for viruses transplant in plants”; the source's answer concerns animal-to-human transplantation.) This is troublesome because of the efforts that are being made to transplant pig tissue into humans (e.g. fetal pig cells into the brains of patients with Parkinson's disease). Transplant recipients must have their immune systems suppressed if the transplant is to avoid rejection. The probability that the original hosts for HIV-1 and HIV-2 were some other primate suggests that retroviruses can move from one species to another.
